lead: After this unit you can read a nonlinear element from its curve, predict a sustained oscillation, sketch a phase portrait, prove stability with a Lyapunov function, and design an LQR gain. The unit connects the frequency-domain and state-space tools you already know to systems that do not obey superposition.
about: This unit leaves the comfort of linear superposition and asks what real systems do at their limits. Chapter 7.1 describes saturation, dead zone and backlash. Chapter 7.2 converts those curves into an amplitude-dependent gain. Chapter 7.3 draws second-order motion as trajectories in the phase plane. Chapter 7.4 explains isolated closed orbits and predicts their amplitude and frequency. Chapter 7.5 proves stability with an energy-like Lyapunov function. Chapter 7.6 chooses a control that minimises a quadratic cost and solves the Riccati equation for the LQR gain.

chapters.idea: Saturation, dead zone and backlash are the three shapes that make a real element stop being a fixed-gain linear block.
chapters.depth: Define a static nonlinearity y=f(x). Saturation: y=kx for |x|≤a, y=±M beyond, with M=ka. Dead zone: y=0 for |x|<δ, then y=k(x−δ) for x>δ and y=k(x+δ) for x<−δ. Backlash: a gap 2b; output follows y=x−b when input increases and y=x+b when it decreases, so it has memory. Sketch all three, give piecewise equations, and explain loop effects: lower effective gain, steady-state error, hunting, limit cycles. Some syllabi call saturation a limiter or clipping, dead zone a deadband, backlash play or lash. Stop before describing-function formulas.

figure.aria: The saturation curve flattens at ±10, the dead zone is flat between ±0.2, and the backlash curve traces a loop of width 0.2.

chapters.example: Three separate elements have: saturation M=10 mA, a=2 mA, k=5; dead zone δ=0.2 mA, k=5; backlash b=0.1 mA. For x=3 mA, find each output; backlash input increases from 0. Answer: saturation y=10 mA; dead zone y=5(3−0.2)=14 mA; backlash y=3−0.1=2.9 mA.
chapters.trap: Backlash is not a single curve: the output depends on direction and starting point. Dead zone removes small signals; saturation limits large signals. Do not mix the two.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 block diagrams; Unit 5 on-off control.
chapters.leave: Describing-function formulas to 7.2; limit-cycle prediction to 7.4.

chapters.idea: A describing function replaces a nonlinear element by a gain N(A) that depends on the amplitude of a sine wave, so a linear frequency-domain test can predict oscillation.
chapters.depth: State assumptions: odd memoryless nonlinearity, sine input A sin ωt, linear plant passes only the fundamental. Define N(A) as fundamental output over input. Give N=k for A≤a and N=(2k/π)[sin⁻¹(a/A)+(a/A)√(1−(a/A)²)] for saturation with A>a. Mention relay N=4M/(πA) and that backlash gives a complex N with phase lag. Stability condition 1+N(A)G(jω)=0; plot G(jω) and −1/N(A); intersection gives limit-cycle amplitude and frequency. Some syllabi call this harmonic linearization or sinusoidal describing function.

figure.aria: The describing function starts at 5 for small amplitudes and falls to about 1.27 at A=10.

chapters.trap: N(A) is not the slope at the origin. The −1/N locus can be a curve with phase; do not treat it as a fixed point.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 Nyquist plot and frequency response; 7.1.
chapters.leave: Exact time simulation; Lyapunov proof to 7.5.

chapters.idea: For a second-order autonomous system, plotting x₂ against x₁ turns every solution into a curve whose shape shows stability.
chapters.depth: Define state plane, phase portrait, vector field, trajectory, equilibrium. Write ẋ₁=x₂, ẋ₂=f(x₁,x₂). Isocline slope dx₂/dx₁=f/x₂; nullclines f=0 and x₂=0. Linearize at equilibrium with Jacobian J=[[0,1],[∂f/∂x₁,∂f/∂x₂]]. Eigenvalues: real same sign node, opposite sign saddle, complex stable focus, imaginary center. Some syllabi call this phase-plane portrait or trajectory method. Keep to two states.

figure.title: Phase-plane procedure
figure.aria: A flowchart goes from state equations to equilibria, Jacobian, eigenvalues and phase portrait.

chapters.example: For ẋ₁=x₂, ẋ₂=−x₁−0.2x₂−x₁³, find the equilibrium at the origin, the Jacobian there, and classify it. Work: x₂=0 and −x₁−x₁³=0 give x₁=0. J at 0 = [[0,1],[-1,-0.2]]. Characteristic λ²+0.2λ+1=0 gives λ=−0.1±j0.995. Stable focus.
chapters.trap: Linearization classifies only a small neighbourhood. A center in the linear model may become a stable or unstable focus in the nonlinear system; check with another method.
chapters.prereq: Unit 6 state space; Unit 2 second-order response.

chapters.idea: A limit cycle is an isolated closed path in the phase plane; nearby paths spiral onto it or away from it, so the oscillation has a fixed amplitude and frequency.
chapters.depth: Define stable, unstable and semi-stable limit cycles. Distinguish from a linear centre (a family of closed orbits) and from a forced response. State Poincaré–Bendixson for plane systems: a closed orbit exists in a bounded region with no equilibrium. Use van der Pol as example. Use describing function to solve 1+N(A)G(jω)=0 for amplitude and frequency. Some syllabi call this self-oscillation or hunting. Keep to second-order and relay examples.

figure.aria: The Nyquist curve of G meets the negative real axis at −1/6, and the relay describing-function line crosses it there, giving a limit cycle.

chapters.example: A relay with output ±1 drives G(s)=1/[s(s+1)(s+2)]. Use N(A)=4/(πA) and find the limit-cycle amplitude A at the relay input and frequency ω. Work: G(jω) denominator is −3ω²+jω(2−ω²). Phase −180° when 2−ω²=0, so ω=√2 rad/s. G(j√2)=−1/6. Condition G=−1/N=−πA/4 gives πA/4=1/6, so A=4/(6π)=0.212.
chapters.trap: The relay output amplitude is 1, but A in N(A) is the amplitude of the sine at the relay input. Do not put 1 for A.
chapters.leave: Stability proof to 7.5; optimal control to 7.6.

chapters.idea: A Lyapunov function is an energy-like V(x) that is positive away from the equilibrium and falls along every trajectory, so stability is proved without solving the equations.
chapters.depth: Define equilibrium, stable, asymptotically stable, globally asymptotically stable. Conditions: V(0)=0, V(x)>0 for x≠0; V̇=∇V·f(x). V̇≤0 gives stability; V̇<0 gives asymptotic stability; V radially unbounded gives global. For linear ẋ=Ax, V=xᵀPx with AᵀP+PA=−Q. Mention Krasovskii method as an alternative. Some syllabi call this the direct method or second method. Stop before optimal control.

figure.title: Lyapunov test
figure.aria: A flowchart tests a positive Lyapunov function: negative derivative gives asymptotic stability, non-positive gives stability.

chapters.example: Show that the origin of ẋ₁=−x₁+x₂, ẋ₂=−x₁−x₂−x₂³ is globally asymptotically stable using V=½(x₁²+x₂²). Work: V>0 for x≠0, V(0)=0, and V is radially unbounded. V̇=x₁(−x₁+x₂)+x₂(−x₁−x₂−x₂³)=−x₁²−x₂²−x₂⁴<0.
chapters.trap: V̇≤0 only proves stability, not asymptotic stability. A positive V with V̇<0 is enough; a negative V is not a Lyapunov function.

chapters.idea: Optimal control chooses u(t) to minimise a cost; for a linear plant and quadratic cost the best control is a state feedback u=−Kx, with K from the Riccati equation.
chapters.depth: Write J=∫₀^∞(xᵀQx+uᵀRu)dt, Q=Qᵀ≥0, R=Rᵀ>0. For ẋ=Ax+Bu, optimal u=−Kx, K=R⁻¹BᵀP, and P solves AᵀP+PA−PBR⁻¹BᵀP+Q=0. Explain trade-off: large Q penalises state error, large R penalises control effort. State that LQR guarantees closed-loop stability when Q≥0, R>0 and the pair (A,B) is controllable. Some syllabi call this LQ control or quadratic regulator. Keep to infinite-horizon continuous form.

figure.title: LQR loop
figure.aria: A loop shows Q and R feeding the Riccati equation, then P and K, then u=−Kx driving the plant and feeding back x.

chapters.example: For ẋ=−x+u with J=∫₀^∞(x²+u²)dt, find the LQR gain and closed-loop pole. Work: A=−1, B=1, Q=1, R=1. ARE gives −2P−P²+1=0, so P²+2P−1=0 and P=−1+√2=0.414. K=R⁻¹BᵀP=0.414. u=−0.414x. Closed loop ẋ=(−1−0.414)x=−1.414x; pole −1.414.
chapters.trap: Take the positive definite solution of the Riccati equation. A negative P gives the wrong sign and an unstable closed loop. R must be positive, not zero.
chapters.prereq: Unit 6 state feedback and controllability; 7.5 Lyapunov quadratic form.
chapters.leave: Nonlinear optimal control and finite-horizon problems to advanced courses.
